title: Final: Ch. 1-10 Review
subtitle: Comprehensive carryover material (~45% of the final)

questions.question: A snack contains 12 g carbohydrate, 5 g protein, and 9 g fat. How many calories does it provide?
questions.explanation: Carbohydrate and protein are 4 kcal/g, fat is 9 kcal/g. (12 x 4) + (5 x 4) + (9 x 9) = 48 + 20 + 81 = 149 kcal.

questions.question: Which of the following supply the body with energy (calories)? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Carbohydrate and protein give 4 kcal/g, fat 9, and alcohol 7. Vitamins, minerals, and water supply no calories - vitamins only help release energy from the macronutrients.

questions.question: Researchers survey 1,504 grocery shoppers one time about their food handling habits and report what percentage follow safe practices. What kind of study is this?
questions.explanation: No treatment was assigned and everyone was measured at a single point in time, which makes it a cross-sectional observational study. It shows prevalence, not cause.

questions.question: Which study design is the only one that can establish that a nutrient actually CAUSES an outcome?
questions.explanation: Random assignment to a treatment is what allows a causal claim. Cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional studies are all observational and can show association only.

questions.question: Which food is the MOST nutrient dense?
questions.explanation: Nutrient density is nutrients per calorie. Plain yogurt delivers protein, calcium, and B vitamins with few calories. Added sweeteners (honey) and solid fats (cream cheese) drive nutrient density down, and juice loses the fiber of whole fruit.

questions.question: Which of the following are stated aims of the Dietary Guidelines for Americans? (Select all that apply)
options: Follow a healthy dietary pattern at every life stage
Choose nutrient-dense foods and beverages with variety
Meet food group needs within calorie limits
Limit added sugars, saturated fat, sodium, and alcohol
Eliminate all carbohydrates from the diet
Take a daily multivitamin regardless of diet quality
questions.explanation: Those four points are the DGA framework, and the overall purpose is to promote health and prevent chronic disease. The Guidelines never call for eliminating a macronutrient or for universal supplementation.

questions.question: Which of these counts as 1 ounce-equivalent from the Protein Foods group?
questions.explanation: 1 egg = 1 oz-eq. Half a cup of beans and 2 Tbsp of peanut butter are each 2 oz-eq, and cheese belongs to the Dairy group, not Protein Foods.

questions.question: Which combination provides exactly 2 cup-equivalents of fruit?
options: 1/2 cup dried mango + 1 1/2 cups frozen pineapple
1/2 cup canned peaches + 1/2 cup raisins + 1 cup orange juice
1/4 cup dried apricots + 3/4 cup apple juice + 1 cup strawberries
questions.explanation: Whole fruit and 100% juice count cup for cup, so 1 + 1 = 2. Dried fruit counts DOUBLE (1/2 cup dried = 1 cup-eq), which pushes the other three options to 2.5, 2.5, and 2.25.

questions.question: On the DRI tables, what does the Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL) tell you?
options: The highest daily intake likely to pose no risk - a ceiling, not a goal
The intake that meets the needs of about 98% of healthy people
The intake that meets the needs of 50% of a group
The amount used as the reference number on a food label
questions.explanation: The UL is a safety ceiling. The RDA (98% of people) is your target, the EAR covers 50% and is used to set the RDA, and the DV is the single label reference based on a 2,000-calorie diet.

questions.question: A cereal label lists 22% DV for iron. How should this be described?
questions.explanation: The 5/20 rule: 5% DV or less is low, 10-19% DV is a 'good source,' and 20% DV or more is 'high in' that nutrient.

flashcards.back: Nutrients supplied per calorie. Calculate as nutrient amount divided by calories per serving. Added sweeteners and solid fats lower it.

flashcards.front: EAR vs RDA vs AI vs UL
flashcards.back: EAR = meets the need of 50% of a group. RDA = meets the need of ~98% (your target). AI = best estimate when data are too thin for an RDA. UL = safety ceiling.
EER = estimated calories to maintain current weight (age, sex, height, weight, activity). AMDR = healthy percentage-of-calories range for each macronutrient.
1 g = 1,000 mg = 1,000,000 mcg. 1 kg = 2.2 lb. 1 inch = 2.54 cm. Always convert to a single unit before comparing.
Ask who profits, whether it is peer-reviewed, whether it promises a quick fix, whether it sells a product, and whether it contradicts the overall body of evidence.
Ingredients are listed in descending order by weight, so the first ingredient tells you what the product is mostly made of.

questions.question: In which organs does chemical digestion of food actually take place? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Only GI tract organs digest food. The liver, gallbladder, and pancreas are accessory organs - they secrete bile and enzymes INTO the small intestine, but no food passes through them and no digestion happens inside them.

questions.question: Which pairing of nutrient, starting organ, and enzyme is correct?
questions.explanation: Carbohydrate digestion begins in the mouth with salivary amylase. Protein digestion begins in the stomach with pepsin (plus HCl to denature), and fat is handled mainly in the small intestine by bile and pancreatic lipase.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes prebiotics from probiotics?
options: Prebiotics are fibers that feed beneficial bacteria; probiotics are the live bacteria themselves
Prebiotics are live bacteria; probiotics are the fibers that feed them
Both terms describe live bacteria found only in yogurt
Prebiotics are antibiotics taken before a meal
questions.explanation: Prebiotics (onions, garlic, bananas, whole grains) are non-digestible fibers that feed gut bacteria. Probiotics (yogurt, kefir, sauerkraut, kimchi) are the live beneficial organisms.

questions.question: An individual with celiac disease must follow which kind of diet?
questions.explanation: Celiac disease is an autoimmune reaction to gluten (wheat, rye, barley) that flattens the intestinal villi and causes malabsorption. The only treatment is a lifelong strict gluten-free diet.

questions.question: Lactose is composed of which two monosaccharides?
questions.explanation: Lactose = glucose + galactose. Sucrose = glucose + fructose, and maltose = glucose + glucose.

questions.question: Which are documented benefits of adequate dietary fiber? (Select all that apply)
options: Slows glucose absorption and blunts blood sugar spikes
Adds bulk and softness to stool, preventing constipation
Promotes satiety and helps with weight management
questions.explanation: Fiber lowers LDL, slows glucose absorption, prevents constipation and diverticular disease, and increases fullness. It supplies no amino acids and it reduces cholesterol absorption rather than increasing it. Fiber is found only in plant foods.

questions.question: What is the key difference between an enriched grain and a whole grain?
options: Enrichment adds back B vitamins and iron but NOT fiber; whole grains keep all three kernel parts
Enriched grains contain more fiber than whole grains
Enriched and whole grain mean the same thing on a label
Whole grains have had the bran and germ removed
questions.explanation: Refining strips the bran and germ. Enrichment restores certain B vitamins and iron but never the fiber, so enriched is not the same as whole grain. Check the first ingredient - 'wheat flour' and 'multigrain' are marketing, not proof.

questions.question: A patient reports gas, bloating, and diarrhea after drinking milk, but has no trouble with hard cheese and small amounts of yogurt. What is going on and how is it managed?
options: Lactose intolerance from low lactase; manage with low-lactose dairy, lactase pills, and smaller spread-out portions
Milk allergy; all dairy must be strictly eliminated
Celiac disease; a gluten-free diet is needed
Lactose intolerance; all dairy must be strictly eliminated
questions.explanation: Lactose intolerance is an enzyme shortage with GI-only symptoms and is dose-dependent, so aged cheese and yogurt are usually tolerated. A milk allergy is an immune reaction to milk protein with multi-system symptoms (hives, swelling, breathing trouble) requiring strict avoidance.

flashcards.back: Insulin LOWERS blood glucose by moving it into cells. Glucagon RAISES it by breaking down liver glycogen.
Type 1: autoimmune loss of insulin production, managed with insulin matched to carbohydrate intake. Type 2: insulin resistance, managed with diet, weight loss, activity, and oral medication.

flashcards.front: Complications of chronic high blood glucose
flashcards.back: Kidney failure, blindness, nerve damage, heart disease, poor wound healing and amputation. NOT anemia.
Starch = plant storage. Glycogen = animal storage in liver and muscle. Fiber/cellulose = indigestible structural carbohydrate.
Glycogen breaks down first, then gluconeogenesis makes glucose from amino acids, then fat breakdown produces ketones. Adequate carbohydrate spares protein.
No digestive enzymes. Absorbs water and electrolytes; bacteria ferment fiber into short-chain fatty acids and gas and make some vitamin K and biotin.
45-65% of total calories, at 4 kcal/g.
Whole grains over refined, whole fruit over juice, skins on, add legumes, nuts and seeds. Increase gradually and add fluid.

questions.question: Which food is highest in cholesterol?
questions.explanation: Cholesterol is a sterol found only in animal foods, and tuna is the only animal product listed. Coconut oil is the trap - it is very high in saturated fat but, being a plant, it contains zero cholesterol.

questions.question: Which food is the best source of EPA and DHA omega-3 fatty acids?
questions.explanation: EPA and DHA come from fatty fish. Plant sources like flaxseed, walnuts, and chia supply ALA. Olive oil is mostly monounsaturated and peanut butter is mono plus omega-6.

questions.question: Which lipoprotein picks up cholesterol from the tissues and returns it to the liver?
questions.explanation: HDL does reverse transport - Healthy, Home to the liver. LDL delivers cholesterol to tissues and artery walls, VLDL carries liver-made triglycerides out, and chylomicrons carry dietary fat from the intestine.

questions.question: After a fatty meal, absorbed fat is packaged into chylomicrons that first enter which system?
options: The portal vein to the liver
questions.explanation: Chylomicrons are too large to enter capillaries directly, so they travel through the lymph before draining into the bloodstream. Water-soluble nutrients like amino acids and glucose go straight to the liver via the portal vein.

questions.question: Why is a saturated fat solid at room temperature while an unsaturated fat is liquid?
options: Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds, so the straight chains pack tightly together
Saturated fats contain more cholesterol, which hardens them
Unsaturated fats contain water, which keeps them liquid
Saturated fats have more double bonds, which stiffens the chain
questions.explanation: No double bonds means straight chains that stack tightly, so the fat is solid. Double bonds create kinks that prevent tight packing, so unsaturated fats stay liquid - and more double bonds also means more prone to rancidity.

questions.question: Which of the following are risk factors for cardiovascular disease? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: High LDL, low HDL, smoking, high blood pressure, inactivity, diabetes, obesity, age, and family history all raise risk. Fiber and regular exercise are protective.

questions.question: Which food provides high quality (complete) protein?
questions.explanation: Complete proteins contain all nine essential amino acids: all animal foods plus soy. Grains, nuts, seeds, and most plant milks are incomplete, which is why complementary pairs like rice and beans matter.

questions.question: Danielle is a 21-year-old female who weighs 120 lbs. What is her RDA for protein?
questions.explanation: 120 lb divided by 2.2 = 54.5 kg, times the RDA of 0.8 g/kg = 43.6, or about 44 g/day. Height is never part of the protein RDA calculation.

questions.question: A child eating enough calories but almost no protein develops a swollen belly and fatty liver. What is this?
questions.explanation: Kwashiorkor is protein deficiency with adequate calories, and the edema comes from too little blood protein to hold fluid in the vessels. Marasmus is deficiency of BOTH calories and protein, producing severe wasting instead.

questions.question: A man wants to order a direct-to-consumer DNA test and then pick a diet based on the results. What is the accurate assessment of this plan?
options: Current consumer genetic tests have limited power to predict disease, since risk comes from many genes plus lifestyle
Genetic testing now reliably determines exactly which diet each person should follow
Genes fully determine chronic disease risk, so diet changes would not help him
Genetic testing can diagnose heart disease and diabetes before symptoms appear
questions.explanation: Nutrigenomics is real - nutrients affect gene expression and genes affect nutrient response - but direct-to-consumer tests currently offer only rough guidance. Established behaviors like more produce, less saturated fat, and regular activity do far more.

flashcards.back: Linoleic (omega-6) and linolenic (omega-3). The body cannot make them, so they must come from food.
Fatty and red meat, butter, cheese, lard, plus the two plant exceptions: palm oil and coconut oil.
Mostly in the small intestine. Bile (made in the liver, stored in the gallbladder) emulsifies fat; pancreatic lipase does the chemical breakdown.
20-35% of calories from fat. AHA: keep saturated fat around 5-6% of calories and minimize trans fat.
It contains nitrogen in addition to carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. There are 20 amino acids and 9 are essential.
Heat, acid, or agitation unfolds a protein's shape and destroys its function - cooking an egg, stomach acid. Generally irreversible.
Positive = building tissue (growth, pregnancy, muscle gain). Equilibrium = healthy stable adult. Negative = losing tissue (illness, injury, starvation).
Build and repair tissue, enzymes, hormones, antibodies, fluid balance, acid-base balance, transport, and energy only as a last resort.
B12 (animal foods only), iron, zinc, calcium, vitamin D, and omega-3s.

questions.question: Which of the following is included in basal metabolism?
questions.explanation: Basal metabolism is what keeps you alive at rest - heartbeat, breathing, nerve activity, body temperature, organ function - and accounts for 60-70% of energy output. Digestion is the separate thermic effect of food (~10%), and activity is its own component.

questions.question: A woman is 5'5" (65 inches) and weighs 130 pounds. What is her BMI?
questions.explanation: BMI (imperial) = lb divided by inches squared, times 703. 130 / 4,225 = 0.03077, times 703 = 21.6, which falls in the normal range of 18.5-24.9.

questions.question: Which statement about BMI and fat distribution is accurate?
options: BMI does not measure body fat directly, and upper-body (visceral) fat carries higher disease risk than lower-body fat
BMI accurately measures body fat percentage in every population
Lower-body 'pear' fat carries the highest risk of heart disease and diabetes
Waist circumference adds no information beyond BMI
questions.explanation: A muscular person can read as overweight and an older adult who has lost muscle can read normal while carrying excess fat. Visceral 'apple' fat around the abdomen raises heart disease and diabetes risk; waist circumference over 40 inches (men) or 35 inches (women) is the red flag.

questions.question: Which are evidence-based strategies for achieving and maintaining a healthy weight? (Select all that apply)
options: Aim for slow, steady loss of 1-2 pounds per week
Focus on sustainable lifestyle change rather than a short-term diet
Control portion sizes and choose nutrient-dense foods
Be physically active most days of the week
Follow a very low calorie crash diet until the goal weight is reached
questions.explanation: Gradual loss, sustainable habits, portion control, and regular activity are what hold. Crash dieting also lowers BMR as the body conserves energy, and weight returns once old habits resume.

flashcards.back: Basal metabolism ~60-70%, physical activity ~15-30% (most variable), thermic effect of food ~10%.
More lean muscle mass, growth, pregnancy, fever, stress, caffeine and nicotine, cold exposure, larger body size, thyroid hormone.
Aging, loss of muscle, and low-calorie dieting or fasting (the body conserves energy).
Under 18.5 underweight, 18.5-24.9 normal, 25-29.9 overweight, 30 and above obese.

questions.question: A patient taking high-dose supplements develops facial flushing and tingling skin. Which nutrient problem is this?
questions.explanation: Flushing is the signature of niacin TOXICITY (along with liver damage at high doses). Niacin DEFICIENCY is pellagra, remembered as the 4 D's: diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia, death.

questions.question: Why is excess folate intake risky for an older adult?
options: It corrects the anemia of B12 deficiency while irreversible nerve damage keeps progressing undetected
It causes neural tube defects in adults
It blocks iron absorption in the small intestine
It builds up in the liver and causes toxicity within days
questions.explanation: Folate masks B12 deficiency. Because both cause macrocytic anemia, extra folate fixes the blood picture while the demyelination continues, which is why folate has an upper limit. Older adults are already at risk because low stomach acid impairs food-bound B12 absorption.

questions.question: Which pairing of vitamin D deficiency to the correct age group is right?
options: Rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults
Osteomalacia in children, rickets in adults
Rickets in both children and adults
Scurvy in children, osteoporosis in adults
questions.explanation: Rickets is the childhood form with bowed legs and soft growing bone; osteomalacia is the adult form. Vitamin D's RDA is 15 mcg (600 IU) for ages 19-70 and rises to 20 mcg after 70.

questions.question: Which are established functions of vitamin C? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Vitamin C builds collagen, acts as an antioxidant, supports immunity, and strongly enhances non-heme iron absorption. Blood clotting is vitamin K, and oxygen transport is iron in hemoglobin. Vitamin C deficiency is scurvy.

questions.question: A man who drinks large amounts of carrot juice develops yellow-orange skin. His sclerae (whites of the eyes) are white and his bilirubin is normal. What is this?
options: Jaundice from vitamin A toxicity - liver damage
questions.explanation: Beta-carotene is provitamin A and its conversion is regulated, so it cannot cause vitamin A toxicity - only orange skin. The discriminator versus jaundice is the sclerae: white in carotenodermia, yellow in jaundice.

questions.question: Which factors ENHANCE absorption of non-heme iron? (Select all that apply)
options: Vitamin C eaten at the same meal
MFP factor from meat, fish, or poultry
Cooking in a cast iron pan
Tea or coffee with the meal
A calcium supplement with the meal
questions.explanation: Vitamin C, MFP factor, cast iron cookware, and low stores all increase non-heme iron absorption. Tannins in tea and coffee, calcium, zinc, phytates, and oxalates all inhibit it.

questions.question: When blood calcium falls, what happens?
options: PTH rises, activates vitamin D, increases absorption, decreases urinary loss, and pulls calcium from bone
Calcitonin rises and pulls calcium out of the blood into bone
Blood calcium simply stays low until dietary calcium increases
The kidneys excrete more calcium to restore balance
questions.explanation: The body defends blood calcium at the bone's expense, which is exactly why chronic calcium deficiency shows up as osteoporosis rather than a low lab value. Calcitonin does the reverse when blood calcium is too high.

questions.question: A teenage boy shows growth failure, poor wound healing, and delayed sexual maturation. Which mineral deficiency fits best?
questions.explanation: Delayed sexual maturation plus poor growth and wound healing is the zinc signature. Iron deficiency gives weakness, fatigue, and pallor; iodine gives goiter; calcium gives osteoporosis.

questions.question: Which are MODIFIABLE risk factors for osteoporosis? (Select all that apply)
options: Low calcium and vitamin D intake
Lack of weight-bearing and resistance exercise
questions.explanation: Sex, age, menopause, family history, small frame, and ethnicity are non-modifiable. Note that swimming and cycling do not count as weight-bearing, and peak bone mass built by the late 20s is the best long-term protection.

flashcards.back: KADE: A, D, E, K. Absorbed with fat, stored in liver and adipose, real toxicity risk. Water-soluble B's and C are excreted in urine and need regular intake.
Steam or microwave briefly, minimal water, skins on, cut just before cooking. The enemies are heat, light, air, water, and long storage.
Non-nutrient plant compounds (lycopene, sulforaphane, isoflavones, catechins). Not essential, no deficiency disease, plants only. They and antioxidants are the dietary factors that lower cancer risk.
Cheilosis (cracked mouth corners) and glossitis (smooth sore tongue). Milk is the signature source, and light destroys it - hence opaque cartons.
Beriberi with edema and nerve and heart problems. Alcohol abuse is the classic U.S. cause.
Animal foods only, so vegans are at risk. Needs intrinsic factor from the stomach - without it, pernicious anemia. Builds myelin; stored in the liver for years.
Meat, poultry, and fish, plus enriched grains. The body can also make niacin from tryptophan.
Initiation (DNA damage), promotion (damaged cells multiply - where diet acts most), progression (growth, invasion, metastasis).
Older adults (blunted thirst) and infants. Also athletes, people with vomiting or diarrhea, and uncontrolled diabetes.
Tap is EPA-regulated and usually fluoridated. Bottled is FDA-regulated, not inherently safer, and usually has no fluoride.

Phytates (whole grains, legumes), oxalates (spinach, rhubarb), tannins (tea, coffee), and competing minerals. Spinach looks calcium-rich but oxalates block it - kale, bok choy, and broccoli are the bioavailable greens.
Sodium: fluid balance and nerve impulses, NOT bone. ~70% comes from processed food, and excess raises blood pressure and urinary calcium loss. Potassium LOWERS blood pressure.
Produce, whole grains, and low-fat dairy, giving high potassium, calcium, and magnesium plus reduced sodium. Normal BP is under 120/80; stage 1 hypertension starts at 130/80.
Iodine makes thyroid hormone; deficiency causes goiter and cretinism in infants. Fluoride hardens enamel and prevents caries; excess during tooth formation causes fluorosis.

questions.question: As exercise shifts from a 100-meter sprint to a two-hour run, how does the fuel mix change?
options: Stored ATP and creatine phosphate, then carbohydrate, then an increasing share of fat
Fat first, then carbohydrate, then protein
Protein is the primary fuel throughout endurance exercise
Carbohydrate is the only fuel used at any intensity
questions.explanation: The first ~10 seconds run on stored ATP and creatine phosphate, short intense work runs on glycogen through anaerobic glycolysis, and longer lower-intensity work uses progressively more fat. Training makes muscle burn more fat at a given workload, which spares glycogen and delays hitting the wall.

questions.question: An athlete is doing a 90-minute training session in the heat. What should she drink during it?
options: A sports drink with 6-8% carbohydrate plus electrolytes
Plain water only, since the session is under two hours
Nothing until the session is over
questions.explanation: Water is fine under 60 minutes. Beyond 60 minutes or in heavy heat, a sports drink supplies carbohydrate and replaces sodium. Afterward, rehydrate with 2-3 cups (16-24 oz) per pound of body weight lost.

questions.question: Which statement about RED-S (Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport) is accurate?
options: It stems from chronic low energy availability and affects athletes of any sex across hormonal, bone, immune, and performance systems
It affects only female athletes and involves only menstrual dysfunction
It is caused by consuming too much protein
It only affects endurance athletes over age 40
questions.explanation: RED-S expanded the older female athlete triad (disordered eating, amenorrhea, low bone density) to recognize that chronic under-fueling harms athletes of any sex across many body systems.

flashcards.back: 150 minutes per week of moderate aerobic activity (or 75 vigorous) PLUS muscle-strengthening on 2 or more days per week.
1.2-2.0 g/kg/day, spread as 20-30 g per meal every 3-4 hours. Even distribution beats one big post-workout dose, and excess is stored as fat.
1-4 hours before: high carbohydrate, low fat, low fiber, moderate protein, familiar foods, plenty of fluid.
Carbohydrate plus protein within about 2 hours, along with fluid and electrolytes. Chocolate milk hits all three.
Iron (sweat losses, foot-strike hemolysis, menstruation) and calcium plus vitamin D (stress fractures).
